Abstract

Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.

I Introduction

Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have fueled an explosive proliferation of multimodal agents [1, 2, 3, 4], spawning a flourishing spectrum of self-evolution techniques across multimodal reasoning [5, 6, 7, 8], multimodal generation [9, 10, 11, 12, 13], GUI and Web navigation [14, 15, 16, 17], and embodied manipulation [18, 19, 20, 21]. Despite strong scenario-specific gains, existing self-evolving methods are designed and evaluated within single scenarios, and their mechanisms do not transfer equally well in both directions of a scenario pair. For example, majority voting derives label-free rewards for reasoning tasks from consistency across sampled answers [22, 5, 23], yet finds no counterpart in embodied manipulation, where action trajectories admit no equivalence check and physical rollouts incur steep execution and reset costs. Conversely, world models circumvent expensive environmental interactions via imagined rollouts [24, 25], but raise a factor that is not scarce in reasoning, where sampling directly from the policy costs little. Beneath this directional breakdown in mechanism transferability, which suggests a cross-scenario asymmetry, also lies a shared self-evolving loop across diverse tasks. Specifically, across all four scenarios, self-evolving agents share the same cycle, i.e., generating exploratory experience, acquiring evaluative feedback, and consolidating persistent updates. This survey investigates the structural source of cross-scenario asymmetry by characterizing this shared loop and explaining why the two directions of a scenario pair meet different obstacles to transfer.

However, as summarized in Table I, existing work leaves this cross-scenario asymmetry unaddressed. Primary studies benchmark exclusively within specific scenarios [40, 20], while prior surveys either overlook the self-evolving loop as an analytical object [1, 2, 3, 41, 42] or formalize it as scenario-agnostic [28, 31, 33]. Even the closest related work [29] attributes verifiable feedback and retraining costs to domain-level paradigms, not to specific mechanisms. To fill this gap, we first formalize the surveyed object through a genus and a differentia. The genus comprises autonomous learning loops satisfying four criteria: (i) autonomy, where the agent operates without human intervention across goals, actions, feedback, and updates post-initialization; (ii) freshness, where experience is generated under the current policy; (iii) durability, where updates persist beyond the episode boundary; and (iv) recurrence, where the loop iterates across cycles. The differentia, self-reference, requires the agent to realize at least one component of its own loop: the goal sampler, the feedback function, or the evolution operator. Loops in the genus lacking self-reference, termed fixed loops, serve as controls across all scenarios to disentangle scenario-imposed constraints from the intrinsic effects of self-evolution.

To locate where a mechanism can transfer, we adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop as our analytical framework, decomposing each cycle into experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation. We formalize each stage’s bottleneck through two governing factors: (i) rollout count and information gain, (ii) feedback fidelity and credit localization, and (iii) retention and generalization. Each scenario imposes ceilings on the rollouts affordable per cycle (K¯\bar{K}) and the feedback fidelity attainable by admissible evaluators (F¯\bar{F}), which span a two-dimensional positioning matrix. In this matrix, multimodal reasoning is situated where both ceilings are high, multimodal generation where F¯\bar{F} is low, GUI and Web navigation where K¯\bar{K} is low, and embodied manipulation where both are low, with simulation raising both ceilings. Comparing self-evolving and fixed loops within each cell further separates the limits imposed by scenario ceilings from those incurred by self-evolving design, e.g., replacing answer keys with sampled consensus in reasoning [22, 5]. The matrix thus identifies which ceilings bind in each scenario, but alone cannot determine whether a given mechanism is portable.

Building on this matrix, we formulate each self-evolving mechanism as a trade-off, in which the agent raises a scarce factor by replacing a fixed component with its own records, proposals, judgments, or memory writes, at the price of presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes. In a target scenario, a mechanism is thus portable if the target holds this resource, conditional if it holds the resource only for a sub-family or after adaptation, blocked if the outcome to be judged is unobservable, and redundant if the raised factor is not scarce. We attribute the cross-scenario asymmetry structurally to the different combinations of scarce factors and resources that the two directions of a scenario pair encounter: e.g., voting finds no output equivalence in manipulation, whereas world models raise a factor that is not scarce in reasoning. These verdicts, inferred from single-scenario evidence and not yet tested, define testable preconditions, not empirical guarantees. A gain over a budget-matched ablation without self-evolution would overturn any verdict that predicts no benefit from an unadapted transfer, which turns these predictions into a concrete measurement agenda.

This paper makes four contributions, the first two to the survey and the last two to the analysis.

  1. ✜

    A condition-based definition and paradigm demarcation. We operationalize autonomy and the differentia through a provenance matrix that records which party realizes each loop component, and apply the definition to sixteen neighboring paradigms, of which five fall outside the genus, two never satisfy the differentia, five are divided by it, and four are self-evolving by definition.

  2. ✜

    A stage-resolved review and positioning matrix. We review each scenario through the three-stage self-evolving loop, place the four scenarios in the positioning matrix, contrast self-evolving with fixed loops in each cell, and trace five degradation modes along the cross-cycle paths through which they propagate.

  3. ✜

    Directed portability across scenario pairs. We recast the mechanisms of all four scenarios as trade-offs and assign each a portability verdict for every target scenario, yielding a structural account of the cross-scenario asymmetry.

  4. ✜

    A falsifiable measurement agenda. We review the evaluation of task-solving capability, self-evolving capability, and judges, and identify the measurements whose absence leaves untestable three claims, i.e., that a gain stems from self-evolution, that a scenario occupies its assigned position, and that the verdicts hold.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II defines the surveyed object, and Sec. III develops the three-stage loop and the positioning matrix. Secs. IV, V, VI and VII review the four scenarios, and Sec. VIII derives the portability verdicts. Finally, Sec. IX treats evaluation, and Secs. X and XI discuss open challenges and conclude.

II Preliminaries

Conceptually, a multimodal agent is a goal-directed decision-making system that interacts with an external environment through a closed perception-cognition-action loop over heterogeneous observation and scenario-specific action spaces [43]. We restrict the scope to agents whose cognitive core is a large (multimodal) foundation model [44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51] extended via interface [52, 53, 54], memory [55], and tools [56, 57, 58, 59], excluding architectures lacking such a core, such as world-model planners and task-specific visuomotor policies. Since the environment supplies perceptions, accepts actions, and specifies goals, we adopt multimodal agent-environment interaction as our formal scaffold. To systematically diagnose the cross-scenario asymmetry, we unfold this loop across two temporal scales: a micro-scale capturing step-by-step behaviors within a single episode, and a macro-scale tracking the cycle-by-cycle evolution of the agent’s own components over long-term experiences. The resulting dual-scale dynamics are formalized under goal-conditioned partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) [60, 61]. On this scaffold, we define the surveyed object across four levels, from the static agent and environment through the learning loop and the autonomous learning loop to the self-evolving loop.

II-A Multimodal Agent

We formulate the static architecture of a multimodal agent as a four-component tuple 𝒜\mathcal{A} (Sec. II) and its environment as a goal-conditioned, modality-decomposed POMDP 𝒫g\mathcal{P}_{g} (Sec. II). The multimodality condition of Sec. II requires Φθ\Phi_{\theta} to directly encode or decode a non-textual channel without intermediate text conversion, such as screen pixels, camera frames, generated images or videos, or low-level motor commands. Under this criterion, an agent perceiving a web page solely through its HTML or accessibility tree is text-only despite rendered visual content.

II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent

Informally, a self-evolving multimodal agent improves its persistent components across cycles without human input post-initialization, learns from experience generated under its own policy, and internally realizes at least one improvement driver: selecting its goals, deriving its feedback, or authoring its updates. We formalize the agent and its environment as the triples ℰ𝒜\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{A}} (Sec. II-A) and ℰℰ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{E}} (Sec. II-A).

Macro-Scale Learning Loop.   Across episodes, the macro-scale frame (Figure 1) wraps interactions into agent-updating cycles. Starting from 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}, each cycle kk passes through goal sampling, rollout, evaluation, and update:

ℋk→σω𝒈k→p𝒈kπ𝒜k𝒟k→VνVν​(𝒟k)→fζ𝒜k+1,\mathcal{H}_{k}\xrightarrow{\sigma_{\omega}}\boldsymbol{g}_{k}\xrightarrow{p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{\boldsymbol{g}_{k}}}\mathcal{D}_{k}\xrightarrow{V_{\nu}}V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})\xrightarrow{f_{\zeta}}\mathcal{A}_{k+1}, (5)

where 𝒈k\boldsymbol{g}_{k} denotes the goal batch drawn from σω​(k,ℋk)\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k}) with support 𝒢k⊆𝒢\mathcal{G}_{k}\!\subseteq\!\mathcal{G}, rollout law p𝒈kπ𝒜kp^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{\boldsymbol{g}_{k}} applies pgπ𝒜kp^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g} across each g∈𝒈kg\in\boldsymbol{g}_{k}, and 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} aggregates the resulting goal-trajectory pairs (with single goals corresponding to unit batch size). The history then extends to ℋk+1=(𝒜0:k+1,𝒟0:k,Vν(𝒟0:k))\mathcal{H}_{k+1}=(\mathcal{A}_{0:k+1},\mathcal{D}_{0:k},V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{0:k})), recording realized scores, stochastic evaluator outputs being non-recoverable from trajectories alone and failure-conditioned samplers conditioning directly on realized values. We designate this recursive mapping a learning loop. The term denotes the cross-cycle structure without presupposing monotonic gains in J⁡(𝒜k,μ𝒢)J(\mathcal{A}_{k};\mu_{\mathcal{G}}), and excludes within-episode adaptation (e.g., in-context learning), which remains confined to ℳshort\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{short}}. A cycle is one iteration of this mapping. When training proceeds in explicit rounds (each regenerating tasks, evaluator states, or rollouts via the antecedent agent before optimization), a cycle corresponds to one round, whose internal optimizer steps form within-cycle optimization under fζf_{\zeta}. In round-free regimes, such as online reinforcement learning drawing fresh rollouts at every optimizer step, each step executes the full mapping as a degenerate cycle.

Meta-Operators and Substrate.  We designate σω\sigma_{\omega}, VνV_{\nu}, and fζf_{\zeta} the three meta-operators of the loop, each acting on whole episodes at the macro scale. Across multimodal scenarios, the goal sampler draws from a fixed task pool [62], poses questions about unlabeled images [5], reselects GUI tasks by historical success [17], or synthesizes simulated scenes [63]. The feedback function verifies discrete answers [64], inspects generated images via the internal understanding pathway [10], queries a vision-language judge on the final screen [14], or evaluates simulator success predicates [62]. The evolution operator updates Φθ\Phi_{\theta} via policy gradient [65] or writes lessons, skills, and memory entries [66, 67, 68]. Auxiliary agents enter either as self-play opponents sampled via the task argument (Sec. II-A) [7] or as learned proposer-solver roles instantiated within Φθ\Phi_{\theta} [22]. The substrate denotes the persistent components that fζf_{\zeta} modifies across cycles [28, 31]. Specifically, a parametric loop updates Φθ\Phi_{\theta} alone, a non-parametric loop modifies only ℳlong\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{long}}, 𝒯\mathcal{T}, or ℐ\mathcal{I} under fixed θ\theta (training-free), and a mixed loop alters both [69, 70].

Expected Evaluation Return.  We evaluate a learning loop at each cycle via its expected return under the evaluation distribution μ𝒢\mu_{\mathcal{G}}, which lies outside the control of σω\sigma_{\omega} to prevent samplers from inflating performance through easier goals. With cycles counted in rounds by some methods and in optimizer steps by others, nn cycles span horizons of different lengths, and the return is therefore reported per cycle. With 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} itself random, depending on the goals, rollouts, and feedback recorded in ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k}, the expectation at cycle kk also ranges over this history,

𝒥k=𝔼ℋk,g∼μ𝒢​[J⁡(𝒜k,g)],k∈ℕ.\mathcal{J}_{k}\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}_{k},\,g\,\sim\,\mu_{\mathcal{G}}}\!\left[\,J(\mathcal{A}_{k};\,g)\,\right],\quad k\in\mathbb{N}. (6)

This sequence evaluates against the idealized reward RR (Eq. 4), whereas the loop ascends the proxy VνV_{\nu}.

II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops

To distinguish it from general learning loops, we formalize the self-evolving loop through a genus of four operational criteria and a differentia of self-reference.

The Genus: Autonomous Learning Loops. We adopt four criteria to bound the genus of autonomous learning loops. Autonomy bars human input across all three meta-operators and rollout actions, whereas freshness, durability, and recurrence respectively exclude static datasets, episodic buffer writes, and uniterated single-shot updates:

  1. 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1}

    Autonomy.  Autonomy requires the loop to operate without human intervention across its meta-operators and action stream post-initialization. Formally, at every cycle k≥0k\!\geq\!0, the goals 𝒈k\boldsymbol{g}_{k}, the signal Vν​(𝒟k)V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k}), and the update of fζf_{\zeta} consume no annotation, verdict, or approval added by a human while the loop runs, and no human-issued action, such as a teleoperated correction, enters 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}. Artifacts fixed prior to cycle 00 (task sets, verification checkers, answer keys, external evaluators and judges, or optimizers) constitute the bootstrap. Human resets modifying 𝒫g\mathcal{P}_{g} and not the learning loop itself, autonomy does not imply reset-free execution [71], and reset overhead is documented separately.

  2. 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}

    Freshness.  Freshness requires per-cycle experience to be drawn from the agent’s current policy, not from a fixed dataset or an external stream. Formally, the cycle-kk distribution depends on 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} through π𝒜k\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}, admitting on-policy sampling 𝒟k∼p𝒈kπ𝒜k\mathcal{D}_{k}\!\sim\!p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{\boldsymbol{g}_{k}} and asynchronous variants whose behavior policy lags 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} by a bounded number of updates, but excluding any agent-independent pstaticp_{\mathrm{static}} [31]. Experience collected once by 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} and reused in later cycles fails the criterion. Generating on-policy rollouts, however, satisfies freshness without constituting self-reference.

  3. 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3}

    Durability.  Durability requires the update to alter the agent beyond the episode boundary. Formally, 𝒜k+1=fζ​(𝒜k,ℋk,𝒟k,Vν​(𝒟k))\mathcal{A}_{k+1}\!=\!f_{\zeta}(\mathcal{A}_{k},\mathcal{H}_{k},\mathcal{D}_{k},V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})) must modify persistent components (Φθk\Phi_{\theta_{k}}, long-term memory ℳlong⊆ℳk\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{long}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{k}, toolset 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k}, or interface ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k}), thereby altering induced policy π𝒜k+1\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k+1}} on at least one goal. This excludes adaptation confined to the within-episode buffer ℳshort\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{short}} and updates restricted to auxiliary proposers or evaluators, which belong to Φθ\Phi_{\theta} yet occupy parameters that π𝒜\pi_{\mathcal{A}} does not read, while admitting memory writes, tool additions, and prompt mutations even without any gradient descent [31, 34].

  4. 𝒞4\mathcal{C}_{4}

    Recurrence.  Recurrence requires the loop to close across cycles instead of terminating after a single update. Formally, the map 𝒜k↦𝒜k+1\mathcal{A}_{k}\!\mapsto\!\mathcal{A}_{k+1} of 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3} is iterated over more than one cycle, whether rounds or degenerate cycles, and each output becomes the next cycle’s agent, not a branch discarded after evaluation. This excludes single-pass optimization pipelines (𝒜0↦𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{0}\!\mapsto\!\mathcal{A}_{1}), even if compliant with 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} through 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3}. The criterion presupposes 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3} and, being satisfied by every multi-step online method, discriminates loops only in round-based regimes.

The Differentia: Self-Reference. The four criteria constrain how the loop runs, not who realizes it, a loop being able to satisfy 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1}–𝒞4\mathcal{C}_{4} while every meta-operator is realized outside the agent. The differentia, self-reference (SR), separates self-evolving loops by requiring the agent to internally realize at least one evolutionary meta-operator, marked by SR tags in Figure 1.11 1 Our criteria adapt those of [31, 28, 34] and treat updated components as a descriptive substrate, but enforce a narrower scope. While prior work categorizes learning from environmental or rule-based rewards as reward-based self-evolution [31] or subsumes reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on fixed datasets [28], self-reference excludes these regimes whenever the agent realizes zero meta-operators. It does not require co-evolving environment dynamics [34], evolving inter-agent topologies [28], or lifelong operation (k→∞k\to\infty). Self-reference and the meta-operator clause of autonomy both ask who realizes each meta-operator, and we therefore record their evaluation for a method mm in the provenance matrix 𝚪⁡(m)∈{0,1}3×4\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(m)\in\{0,1\}^{3\times 4}. Its rows index (σω,Vν,fζ)(\sigma_{\omega},V_{\nu},f_{\zeta}) and columns span four provenance classes: runtime human input (h), bootstrap artifacts fixed prior to initialization (b), environment/task generation (e), and the agent (a), with Γi​j​(m)=1\Gamma_{ij}(m)=1 when class jj participates in realizing meta-operator ii (rows admit multiple ones). The a entry is tested under row-specific criteria. The goal-sampler row is marked when σω​(k,ℋk)\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k}) conditions on the agent or its history, as with learned proposers, success-dependent curriculum rules, or self-play opponents drawn via the task argument (Sec. II-A); post-hoc filtering of tied goals leaves subsequent draws unconditioned and is excluded. The feedback row is marked when VνV_{\nu} depends on the agent, through the active policy (self-judges, consensus voting over rollouts, or reward models refitted on trajectories) or frozen snapshots (including the initial agent 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}); group-relative normalization and per-goal monotone transforms add no dependence. Snapshots count because shared model lineage preserves priors, and model-based evaluators reportedly favor their own generations [112], a bias plausibly transmitted to descendant policies. The evolution-operator row is marked when the agent model, its replica, or an internally trained component writes update content beyond raw rollouts, such as a lesson, skill, memory entry, or relabeled goal. This row tests writer provenance, not functional dependence, every fζf_{\zeta} depending trivially on the updated 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}. Promptbreeder [109], which rewrites its own improvement mechanism, is a special case of an a entry in this row. Beyond membership, an a entry tracking the current agent couples successive cycles through shared model parameters or history-conditioned goal rules, whereas a frozen snapshot couples none.

Fixed Loops and Scope.  An autonomous learning loop with self-reference is self-evolving, whereas one lacking it is fixed-loop, completing the membership test in Sec. II-A. Because the subsequent three-stage decomposition, its six factors, the two ceilings, and cross-cycle coupling are defined over autonomous learning loops, fixed-loop methods serve there as evidence characterizing a scenario’s operating point, whereas scenario chapters review self-evolving loops, reporting their provenance rows and design variables. A method can have a entries in several rows (e.g., proposer-solver methods realize both the goal sampler and the feedback function [22, 5]).

II-D Demarcation from Established Paradigms

The term self-evolving shares vocabulary with several established paradigms, and recent surveys draw its boundary at different points [28, 31, 34, 113, 114]. Table II compares adjacent paradigms; contested boundaries hinge on the a entry. In the goal-sampler row, discarding tied groups within a batch adds no a entry [62], whereas allocating subsequent rollouts by task success qualifies [115]. In the evolution-operator row, the test is who writes the update: a separate fixed model (e.g., GPT-4o guiding GPT-3.5-Turbo in TextGrad) keeps the loop fixed [104, 102], whereas the acting model itself, as with ExpeL’s insights [66] or STaR’s rationales for failed instances [92], establishes self-evolution. Reflexion [116], where the acting model preserves self-reflections across episodic trials, qualifies as self-evolving, although its reflections, written for one task, improve no other task. Anti-forgetting mechanisms of continual learning map onto the evolution operator fζf_{\zeta}, whereas classical curriculum samplers such as POET [117], PLR and other regret-based environment designers [118, 119, 120], goal-proposing teachers [121, 122], and expert-iteration and AlphaZero self-play [123, 124] remain outside our foundation-model scope.

III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop

We adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop as our analytical framework, decomposing each cycle of an autonomous learning loop into experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation. Fixed and self-evolving loops across all four scenarios sharing this structure, we differentiate them by where the bottleneck binds instead of by topology, treating rollout cost and feedback fidelity as bounds on viable mechanisms. We first formalize the three stages and their governing factors, then position the four scenarios within a positioning matrix spanned by these bounds, and trace how the stages couple across cycles.

III-A Loop Decomposition

As shown in Figure 2, we factor each cycle into three scenario-invariant stages, each organized around one meta-operator (σω\sigma_{\omega}, VνV_{\nu}, fζf_{\zeta}). This decomposition applies across the entire genus of autonomous learning loops and treats auxiliary operations, such as credit assignment or data filtering, as refinements within a stage, not as additional stages.

  1. Stage 1

    Experience Generation (EG):  the goal sampler σω\sigma_{\omega} draws the goal batch 𝒈k\boldsymbol{g}_{k}, and the current agent 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} rolls out in 𝒫g\mathcal{P}_{g} for each goal g∈𝒈kg\in\boldsymbol{g}_{k}, producing the trajectory batch 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}. Through the quantity and informativeness of 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}, the only trajectories FA and UC act on, EG bounds how fast and how broadly the loop can evolve (speed and breadth).

  2. Stage 2

    Feedback Acquisition (FA):  the feedback function VνV_{\nu} maps 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}, together with the agent history 𝒜0:k\mathcal{A}_{0:k} when VνV_{\nu} reads the agent, to scores, preferences, or critiques sourced from the environment, the bootstrap, or the agent itself. FA is the loop’s only source of information about the idealized task reward RR (the RR-aligned direction).

  3. Stage 3

    Update Consolidation (UC):  the evolution operator fζf_{\zeta} computes an update from (𝒜k,ℋk,𝒟k,Vν​(𝒟k))(\mathcal{A}_{k},\mathcal{H}_{k},\mathcal{D}_{k},V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})) and writes it into at least one persistent component of 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}, producing the next-cycle agent 𝒜k+1\mathcal{A}_{k+1}. UC determines whether an update persists across later cycles and generalizes beyond the goals that produced it (retention and generalization).

The six factors originate at the two scales of Figure 1. The per-episode cost c⁡(τ)c(\tau) governing K¯\bar{K} and action localization LνL_{\nu} arise within the micro-scale interaction loop, whereas information gain, evaluator fidelity FνF_{\nu}, and consolidation factors (SζS_{\zeta}, GζG_{\zeta}) emerge from the macro-scale learning loop, the positioning matrix thereby pairing a micro-scale axis with a macro-scale one.

III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG)

EG produces the trajectory batch 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} of each cycle by rolling out the current agent 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} in the POMDPs 𝒫g\mathcal{P}_{g} of Sec. II-A. For each goal gg in the batch 𝒈k\boldsymbol{g}_{k} drawn from σω​(k,ℋk)\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k}), 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} draws KkK_{k} rollouts from pgπ𝒜kp^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g} and pools them into 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}. EG must supply experience of sufficient scale and informativeness under finite compute, wall-clock, and safety budgets, a constraint on quantity and one on quality. We summarize this bottleneck through an effective-experience decomposition,

𝒬kEG:=Kk⋅𝔼g∼σω​(k,ℋk)​[I𝒜k​(g)],\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{EG}}\;:=\;K_{k}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k})}\!\left[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(g)\right], (9)

where KkK_{k} is the number of per-goal rollouts in cycle kk, and I𝒜k​(g):=Varτ∼pgπ​[retg​(τ)]I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(g)\!:=\!\mathrm{Var}_{\tau\sim p^{\pi}_{g}}[\mathrm{ret}_{g}(\tau)] is the outcome variance of gg. Here, retg​(τ)=∑tγt​R​(st,ut,g)\mathrm{ret}_{g}(\tau)\!=\!\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}R(s_{t},u_{t},g) denotes the return of τ\tau, and pgπp^{\pi}_{g} abbreviates pgπ𝒜kp^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g}. This variance, a goal-level proxy for the learnable information gain [131], vanishes on goals that 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} has mastered or never solves, where GRPO-style group-relative updates receive zero advantage under an RR-aligned evaluator. Under a binary terminal reward with γ=1\gamma\!=\!1, it reduces to pg​(1−pg)p_{g}(1-p_{g}), which difficulty-targeting rewards and filters track via an estimated success probability pgp_{g}. Defined on the idealized reward RR of Eq. 4, the proxy renders 𝒬kEG\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{EG}} diagnostic, and it exposes two failure modes. As KkK_{k} shrinks, too few per-goal rollouts remain to contrast success with failure. As 𝔼⁡[I𝒜k]\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}] approaches zero, the sampled goals are mastered or unreachable. Concretely, KkK_{k} is bounded by per-rollout interaction cost and action recoverability, while 𝔼⁡[I𝒜k]\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}] is governed by the diversity and information gain targeted by σω\sigma_{\omega} and by the interaction mode realizing pgπ𝒜kp^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g} (Table III).

Quantity Constraint.   Interaction cost and action recoverability govern KkK_{k} via a single per-rollout cost c⁡(τ)c(\tau), eliminating the need for a separate term for actions that resist reverting, resetting, or safe repetition. Specifically, c⁡(τ)c(\tau) absorbs the time, compute, synchronization, and reset cost of one rollout, with the reset term penalizing both environment restoration and expected damage from failed trajectories. Under a fixed per-goal budget BB, the rollout count satisfies the affordability ceiling Kk≤K¯:=B/𝔼τ​[c⁡(τ)]K_{k}\!\leq\!\bar{K}\!:=\!B/\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[c(\tau)], where the expectation runs over episodes of the target task family at the horizon cap TmaxT_{\max}, not over the rollouts of a particular policy, which lets K¯\bar{K} reflect task structure and not policy choice. When c⁡(τ)c(\tau) is small, group-sampling operators such as self-consistency [80, 132] or GRPO [65, 133, 134] sample a group of rollouts per goal at negligible marginal cost. As c⁡(τ)c(\tau) grows, the bottleneck shifts from theoretical execution feasibility to the budget of exploratory failures the system can absorb.

Quality Constraint.   Even with a large KkK_{k}, a trajectory set is unproductive if its goals are already mastered or still unreachable for 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}, leaving EG viable only while 𝔼⁡[I𝒜k]>0\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]\!>\!0. For instance, self-play [131] stops improving once its synthetic pipeline no longer supplies learnable information gain. Diversity and information gain determines whether σω\sigma_{\omega} draws goals with nonzero I𝒜kI_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}. Sampling schemes escalate in intervention from random sampling [65] through curriculum mining over past failures [135, 17] and active task selection [136, 137] to environment synthesis [63, 138, 139, 140, 141]. Random sampling keeps σω\sigma_{\omega} stationary, whereas curriculum mining and active selection make it adaptive. Environment synthesis acts through the task argument gg of Sec. II-A and is adaptive only when the generator reads the agent’s record. Only an adaptive sampler conditions the next goal draw on the agent’s record and places an a entry in the goal-sampler row. Interaction mode fixes what evidence each trajectory can expose. Single-pass generation and tool-augmented reasoning yield single-action episodes, whereas digital and embodied environments expose multi-step state transitions whose informativeness depends on platform dynamics, reset conditions, and observability.

Asymmetric Substitutability.   The product in Eq. 9 enables mutual compensation between its two factors, locating the cross-scenario asymmetry in the cost of raising each factor. Raising KkK_{k} offsets low information gain only when rollouts are cheap, parallelizable, and recoverable and feedback retains contrast as group size grows. Consensus rewards losing contrast beyond small groups [22], the loop elsewhere must instead raise 𝔼⁡[I𝒜k]\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}] via curriculum mining [115, 17], active exploration [5, 18], demonstrations at initialization [19], or synthetic environments [6, 63, 138]. Equal values of KkK_{k} therefore do not imply identical bottlenecks. Multimodal generation and GUI/Web navigation report overlapping group sizes (Table III), yet generation samples cheap, reversible passes below K¯\bar{K} and is bounded by 𝔼⁡[I𝒜k]\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}] over a fixed prompt pool, whereas navigation incurs latency-bound episodes and is bounded by K¯\bar{K} itself. Cheap but uninformative rollouts saturate the loop, whereas informative but costly rollouts throttle its scaling.

III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA)

FA maps the trajectory batch 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} of each cycle to the feedback Vν​(𝒟k)∈(𝕐mm)∗V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})\!\in\!(\mathbb{Y}^{\mathrm{mm}})^{*}, the scores, preferences, critiques, or structured judgments that direct fζf_{\zeta}. Any scoring, ranking, filtering, or best-of-NN selection by VνV_{\nu} belongs to FA even when interleaved with generation, whereas VνV_{\nu}-independent filtering such as deduplication remains in EG. FA must supply feedback that is aligned with the intended objective RR and localized at an actionable grain without recurring human supervision (𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1}), a constraint on fidelity and one on localization. We summarize this bottleneck through an effective-feedback decomposition,

𝒬kFA:=(2​Fν​(𝒟k,R,𝒈k)−1)⋅𝔼τ∼p^𝒟k​[Lν​(τ)],\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{FA}}\;:=\;\bigl(2F_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k};R,\boldsymbol{g}_{k})-1\bigr)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{D}_{k}}}\!\left[L_{\nu}(\tau)\right], (10)

where p^𝒟k\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{D}_{k}} is the empirical measure on 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}, Fν∈[0,1]F_{\nu}\!\in\![0,1] is the rate at which the ordering Vν​(𝒟k)V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k}) induces on same-goal trajectory pairs agrees with their ordering by retg\mathrm{ret}_{g}, and Lν​(τ)∈(0,1]L_{\nu}(\tau)\!\in\!(0,1] is the fraction of environment actions along τ\tau to which VνV_{\nu} can assign credit. Here, pairs tied under either ordering are excluded, and Fν:=1/2F_{\nu}\!:=\!1/2 if none remains. This pairwise form covers scalar, pairwise, and ranked feedback alike, and 2​Fν−12F_{\nu}-1 is the Goodman-Kruskal rank correlation of the two orderings, zero for a random evaluator and negative for a reversing one. Like I𝒜kI_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}, FνF_{\nu} is defined on RR, which makes 𝒬kFA\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{FA}} diagnostic, and it exposes two failure modes. As FνF_{\nu} falls toward 1/21/2, fζf_{\zeta} follows an uninformative proxy, and below 1/21/2 it optimizes against RR. As LνL_{\nu} shrinks, a correct signal becomes too coarse to guide improvement. Concretely, FνF_{\nu} is bounded by the signal source and gaming resistance of VνV_{\nu}, while LνL_{\nu} is governed by the temporal granularity and credit-assignment cost of its scores (Table IV).

Fidelity Constraint.   Signal source and gaming resistance act on FνF_{\nu} at different levels: the signal source fixes the evaluator configurations ΞV\Xi_{V} a scenario admits, hence the attainable-fidelity ceiling F¯:=supν∈ΞVFν\bar{F}\!:=\!\sup_{\nu\in\Xi_{V}}F_{\nu}, whereas gaming resistance governs how much of it survives repeated fζf_{\zeta} updates. Where a closed-form success condition or a discrete answer space exists, deterministic instruments such as answers computed by task generation [64, 146], unit tests [147, 148], and physical-constraint rewards [18, 145, 149] sustain high FνF_{\nu} at modest cost. Lacking both, evaluators rely on self-rewards [9, 10, 150, 151], reward models [135, 144, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156], or VLM judges [14, 18, 157, 158], and gaming resistance binds [9, 159]. Channel coverage further caps FνF_{\nu}, an instrument leaving unobserved channels of 𝒰\mathcal{U} unconstrained [9, 18, 145]. Self-rewards and co-trained reward models read 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} and place an a entry in the feedback row, and their realized fidelity Fν(k)F_{\nu}^{(k)} therefore drifts with the policy they score; all others enter as b or e. Reported audits measure label or verdict accuracy aa, not the pairwise agreement that defines FνF_{\nu}. Under a binary terminal reward with verdict errors independent across trajectories and symmetric across outcomes, a success-failure pair is ordered correctly with probability a2a^{2} and reversed with probability (1−a)2(1-a)^{2}, giving Fν=a2/(a2+(1−a)2)F_{\nu}=a^{2}/(a^{2}+(1-a)^{2}), which exceeds aa whenever a>1/2a>1/2. A reported accuracy thus bounds FνF_{\nu} from below only under these assumptions, and errors correlated within a goal void the bound. In multimodal reasoning, program-computed answers stay correct on 94.4% of retained questions [64], yet self-generated pseudo-labels degrade across rounds [5, 160], consistent with self-referential evaluators drifting below a high F¯\bar{F}, although rising question difficulty confounds these declines.

Localization Constraint.   Even with high FνF_{\nu}, a trajectory set is directionally unproductive if LνL_{\nu} covers a vanishing fraction of environment actions, and FA accordingly remains viable only while 𝔼τ​[Lν​(τ)]\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[L_{\nu}(\tau)] suffices for the grain fζf_{\zeta} requires. Temporal granularity fixes the scoring unit along τ\tau: the terminal outcome for episode-level scores, the action utu_{t} for step-level scores, and the output yty_{t} decoded into utu_{t} for token-level scores. Because LνL_{\nu} counts environment actions, a single-action episode has Lν=1L_{\nu}\!=\!1, and credit within a long reasoning chain yty_{t} lies outside LνL_{\nu} even where process reward models assign it [153]. Episode-level feedback suffices when the task reduces to one discrete outcome, step-level process supervision becomes necessary as horizons lengthen and terminal success grows too sparse [153, 167, 168, 18, 169], and token-level credit remains rare outside independently checkable reasoning chains [170]. Credit-assignment cost determines how much of that grain a cycle can afford, step-level scores requiring a process model or per-step estimates whose cost grows with horizon length [153]. Granularity is thus an FA choice that reaches fζf_{\zeta} only through its signal.

Asymmetric Vulnerability.   The product in Eq. 10 admits only conditional, one-directional compensation between its two factors. Higher FνF_{\nu} from cross-model verification or understanding-generation duality offsets moderate localization loss only when an unbiased anchor exists [10, 128], whereas finer LνL_{\nu} yields no directional gain once FνF_{\nu} is gameable [9, 159]. Equal ceilings F¯\bar{F} therefore do not imply identical bottlenecks. Multimodal reasoning and GUI/Web navigation both admit a high F¯\bar{F} (Table IV), through program-computed answers [64] and per-task state scripts in sandboxed environments [115, 17], yet reasoning fixes Lν=1L_{\nu}\!=\!1 and is bounded by the realized Fν(k)F_{\nu}^{(k)} of its consensus and self-judged signals [5, 160, 171], while navigation scores whole long-horizon episodes and is bounded by LνL_{\nu} [16, 135, 144]. Multimodal generation instead faces a low F¯\bar{F} on open-ended prompts, where self-rewards and perception-only instruments are readily gamed [9, 10], and embodied manipulation loses both factors on hardware [172, 173, 19, 145]. Fidelity-bounded signals thus misdirect the loop and localization-bounded ones under-constrain it, making F¯\bar{F} a positioning axis and LνL_{\nu} a within-regime variable.

III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC)

UC writes the update that fζf_{\zeta} computes from 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} and Vν​(𝒟k)V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k}) into one or more persistent components of 𝒜k=(Φθk,ℳk,𝒯k,ℐk)\mathcal{A}_{k}\!=\!(\Phi_{\theta_{k}},\mathcal{M}_{k},\mathcal{T}_{k},\mathcal{I}_{k}), as 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3} requires. Writes to the episode-scoped buffer ℳshort\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{short}} through Ψ\Psi fall outside UC, and VνV_{\nu}-based selection of what to write remains in FA. UC must write updates that persist undegraded across subsequent cycles and generalize beyond the cycle-kk goals, a constraint on retention and one on generalization. We summarize this bottleneck through an effective-consolidation decomposition,

𝒬kUC:=Sζ(𝒜k:k+j+1)⋅Gζ(𝒜k+1;μ𝒢),\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{UC}}\;:=\;S_{\zeta}\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{k:k+j+1}\bigr)\cdot G_{\zeta}\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{k+1};\,\mu_{\mathcal{G}}\bigr), (11)

where Δk​(g)=J⁡(𝒜k+1,g)−J⁡(𝒜k,g)\Delta_{k}(g)\!=\!J(\mathcal{A}_{k+1};g)\!-\!J(\mathcal{A}_{k};g) is the cycle-kk gain on goal gg, 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k} is the support of 𝒈k\boldsymbol{g}_{k}, and μ𝒢\mu_{\mathcal{G}} is the fixed evaluation distribution of Eq. 6. Here, Sζ∈[0,1]S_{\zeta}\!\in\![0,1] is the fraction of the cycle-kk gain on 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k} that survives jj further cycles, min⁡{1,max⁡{0,𝔼g∼μ𝒢|𝒢k​[J⁡(𝒜k+1+j,g)−J⁡(𝒜k,g)]/𝔼g∼μ𝒢|𝒢k​[Δk​(g)]}}\min\{1,\,\max\{0,\,\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\mu_{\mathcal{G}}|\mathcal{G}_{k}}[J(\mathcal{A}_{k+1+j};g)-J(\mathcal{A}_{k};g)]\,/\,\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\mu_{\mathcal{G}}|\mathcal{G}_{k}}[\Delta_{k}(g)]\}\} for a positive denominator, and Gζ∈[0,1]G_{\zeta}\!\in\![0,1] is the μ𝒢\mu_{\mathcal{G}}-measure of goals outside 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k} with Δk​(g)>0\Delta_{k}(g)\!>\!0, renormalized to the complement of 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}. The gain and the two factors correspond to the adaptivity, retention, and generalization goals proposed for self-evolving agents [31], and SζS_{\zeta} normalizes by the cycle-kk gain the change on earlier goals that backward transfer records as a signed difference [94]. Like FνF_{\nu}, both factors are defined through JJ and hence on RR, leaving 𝒬kUC\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{UC}} diagnostic as well, and it exposes two failure modes. As SζS_{\zeta} falls toward zero, later cycles erase or distort the cycle-kk gain. As GζG_{\zeta} falls toward zero, the update stays confined to 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}. Concretely, SζS_{\zeta} is bounded by the substrate that fζf_{\zeta} writes and its iteration robustness, while GζG_{\zeta} is governed by the transfer locus of that substrate and the experience coverage of 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} (Table V).

Retention Constraint.   Substrate and iteration robustness act on SζS_{\zeta} at different levels: the substrate fixes how far a single write can interfere with earlier gains, whereas iteration robustness governs whether those gains survive repeated fζf_{\zeta} applications. The substrate is either Φθ\Phi_{\theta}, written by GRPO [65], PPO [174], or DPO [175], or a non-parametric component such as memory [55, 176, 116, 177, 178], tools [67, 179], or prompts [180, 181, 182]. Three documented failure modes threaten iteration robustness: compounding reward hacking through accumulated Stage 2 bias within single runs [9, 129], distribution shift as the rollout law leaves the calibration region of VνV_{\nu} [14], and catastrophic forgetting through interference in Φθ\Phi_{\theta} [95, 161]. Hacking and shift enter across the cycle boundary, whereas forgetting arises inside fζf_{\zeta} and yields to experience replay, parameter isolation, and regularized updates [95, 161, 183, 184, 185, 186]. Within one task family, the three modes can compound into long-cycle drift, a slow multi-source degradation that terminal-only reporting leaves undetected and per-round scores on a fixed benchmark suite reveal only as non-monotone curves.

Generalization Constraint.   Even with high SζS_{\zeta}, a persisted update confers no broader benefit if it improves only the goals in 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}, UC thus remaining useful only while 𝒜k+1\mathcal{A}_{k+1} improves on a non-trivial share of the goals outside 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}. Transfer locus fixes where a write takes effect: on any goal that activates the affected weights for parameters, upon retrieval for memory, upon invocation for tools, and within the templating scope for prompts. Experience coverage determines the subspace of 𝒢\mathcal{G} to which the update can generalize, and reported gains stay mostly within the support of 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}, as the fixed loops UI-Voyager [187], UI-Mem [104], and an online skill library [164] train and evaluate on the same task sets. Achieved scope rises from in-distribution transfer to unsampled goals of the same regime, through cross-task transfer to neighboring goal subspaces, to cross-domain transfer to other GUI platforms or real hardware, the last reached by few methods on small trial counts [166, 18]. The substrate thus upper-bounds transfer, and the coverage of 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} sets how much of it a cycle realizes.

Within-Regime Specialization.   Neither factor of Eq. 11 has a scenario-fixed ceiling, and UC therefore specializes within each quadrant, not along an axis. SζS_{\zeta} binds when FA is gameable or EG is non-recoverable, and GζG_{\zeta} binds when 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} covers too little of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Shared substrates therefore do not imply identical bottlenecks. Multimodal reasoning and GUI/Web navigation share Φθ\Phi_{\theta} as the dominant substrate (Table V), yet reasoning sustains intensive parametric writes under low-cost EG and rule-checkable FA and is bounded by long-cycle drift [5, 22, 64], while navigation stabilizes its parametric writes by trajectory replay [14, 17] and, in both parametric and training-free forms, is bounded by transfer that stays within one platform. Multimodal generation shares the retention bottleneck through compounding hacking of its parametric writes [9, 129], and embodied manipulation shares the generalization bottleneck, writing to Φθ\Phi_{\theta} and to skills, memory, and harnesses [188, 189, 190, 166] within single simulator suites. Few methods measure either factor across cycles, and retention on earlier-round goals is measured in a single self-evolving loop, RSI in UMMs [191], besides fixed-loop continual reinforcement learning [95, 161]. UC thus inherits its bottleneck from the first two stages and refines a method within its quadrant without moving it.

III-E Cross-Scenario Positioning

The stage analyses locate where each scenario’s loop is bound, and this subsection condenses them into a positioning matrix that accounts for the cross-scenario asymmetry. To serve as an axis, a stage factor must be scenario-exogenous, fixed by task structure instead of algorithmic choice, and substitution-resistant, bounded in a way that the paired factor of its stage cannot relax. Realized values, which each method sets through its budget and evaluator, fail the first condition, leaving the ceilings as the only admissible axes.

Axis Selection.   We select the ceilings K¯\bar{K} and F¯\bar{F} as the two axes, the only stage factors satisfying both conditions. The horizontal axis K¯\bar{K} is fixed by interaction cost and recoverability, and no information-gain intervention lifts it. With BB shared as a comparison convention, not a measured quantity, K¯\bar{K} orders scenarios by 𝔼τ​[c​(τ)]\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[c(\tau)]. The vertical axis F¯\bar{F} is fixed by verifier availability, and no localization refinement raises it. We assess F¯\bar{F} on the task families that define a scenario’s target, such as open-ended prompts in generation and open task sets on hardware in manipulation, excluding sub-families whose closed-form success predicates push the ceiling near one. Its value is the highest fidelity a reported evaluator attains on these families, an estimate that may run high, agreement measured on fixed outputs tending to fall under optimization. The other four factors each fail a condition: the information gain fails scenario-exogeneity, its ceiling supω𝔼⁡[I𝒜k]\sup_{\omega}\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}] being set by backbone coverage; the localization LνL_{\nu} fails substitution-resistance in that a higher FνF_{\nu} offsets its deficit when an unbiased anchor exists; and SζS_{\zeta} and GζG_{\zeta} have no scenario-fixed ceiling.

Quadrant Assignment.   We place each scenario in a quadrant of Figure 3 by the height of its two ceilings, calling a ceiling binding when it is low. Multimodal reasoning faces neither low ceiling, multimodal generation a low F¯\bar{F} on open-ended prompts, GUI/Web navigation a low K¯\bar{K} under latency-bound episodes in sandboxed environments whose end states per-task scripts inspect, and embodied manipulation both in physical deployment, its target. Three displacements, drawn dashed in the matrix, qualify this placement: (i) most embodied loops learn in simulation, where success predicates raise F¯\bar{F} and group sampling eases K¯\bar{K}, shifting the operating point toward the navigation cell; (ii) generation contains verifiable sub-families such as OCR-scored prompts [195, 196, 197, 198, 199] and program-rendered charts [191], raising F¯\bar{F} toward the reasoning cell; and (iii) navigation on live websites or free-form goals lacks state scripts and falls to screenshot judges [101, 200, 201], lowering F¯\bar{F} toward the manipulation cell. The four scenarios thus occupy four quadrants, consistent with the bottom rows of Tables III and IV, and the two off-diagonal cells, cheap but gameable generation and costly but verifiable navigation, are combinations that a single difficulty ordering would merge. In the absence of any study that estimates either ceiling under one definition in more than one scenario, the placement remains inferred from reported operating points.

Backbone Prior as a Confound.   The backbone 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} confounds this placement by bounding what a loop can reach independently of task structure. In text-only models, self-verification sharpens a model toward outputs it already ranks highly [202], reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards narrows the problems solved at large sampling budgets [203], and gains from spurious rewards vary with the model family [204]. Backbones also differ across scenarios, from vision-language models pretrained on large question-answering corpora in reasoning to action policies with far less motor pretraining in manipulation. Part of the contrast that the matrix attributes to K¯\bar{K} and F¯\bar{F} may thus reflect backbone coverage, a factor that stays entangled with task structure.

Feasibility Filter.   The matrix supplies the first of two checks on whether a mechanism transfers across scenarios. Scenario-fixed by construction, the two ceilings bound the rollouts and the fidelity open to any learning loop within a quadrant. A transferred mechanism further presupposes resources of its source scenario that neither ceiling records, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and where the target lacks them, the mechanism is conditional on an adaptation or a sub-family that supplies them. The matrix thus bounds within-cycle feasibility without deciding portability, its verdicts remaining untested while each reported comparison stays confined to one scenario.

III-F Cross-Cycle Coupling

Beyond the matrix’s within-cycle bounds, the recurrence of Eq. 5 couples successive cycles. It feeds two cycle-kk outputs into Stage 1 of cycle k+1k{+}1, the updated agent 𝒜k+1\mathcal{A}_{k+1} that induces the next rollout policy and the extended history ℋk+1\mathcal{H}_{k+1} that conditions the next goal draw, each defining a directed edge across the cycle boundary. Environmental drift, which Sec. II-A holds fixed but live websites exhibit [200, 205], enters as a third path from outside the loop. These paths carry both self-reference and long-run degradation.

Two Coupling Edges.   The two edges differ in carrier and conditionality. The agent edge runs from Stage 3 of cycle kk to Stage 1 of cycle k+1k{+}1, carrying the persisted update into 𝒜k+1\mathcal{A}_{k+1} and hence into the rollout distribution of 𝒟k+1\mathcal{D}_{k+1}. Present in every autonomous learning loop, it supplies the closure on which 𝒞4\mathcal{C}_{4} rests and extends to any further component that reads the current agent: to σω\sigma_{\omega} under a trained proposer [22, 5], to Stage 2 under an evaluator sharing Φθ\Phi_{\theta} [22, 6], rendering Fν(k)F_{\nu}^{(k)} endogenous, and to Stage 3 under a generative model that records lessons or skills [20, 162]. The goal edge runs from Stages 1 and 2 of cycle kk to Stage 1 of cycle k+1k{+}1 through σω​(k+1,ℋk+1)\sigma_{\omega}(k{+}1,\mathcal{H}_{k+1}), carrying the cycle-kk trajectories and their scores into the next goal draw. A stationary or scheduled sampler, reading no cycle-specific signal, leaves this edge inert, whereas an adaptive sampler activates it and superimposes a second feedback loop on the agent edge. Self-reference thus acts through the extensions of the agent edge and through the goal edge: a fixed-loop method retains only the agent edge into Stage 1, and a frozen snapshot satisfies self-reference without opening any of these paths.

Five Degradation Modes.   We interpret long-run degradation through these paths under a mitigation-locality reading, in which the stage where a degradation surfaces, the path that carries it, and the stage where it is best mitigated need not coincide, and Table VI records all three for five modes. Compounding reward hacking and distribution shift travel along the agent edge as the in-support and extrapolation variants of Goodhart’s law [206], which reward-model overoptimization exhibits together [207], with shift also entering along the environment path [14, 200]. Forgetting and plasticity loss follow a moving goal distribution carried by the environment path or the goal edge [192], and the two collapse modes contract the support of EG, curriculum collapse through the goal edge or the agent edge into σω\sigma_{\omega} [131, 5] and model collapse through the agent edge under any sampler [193]. The three loci diverge most for hacking and forgetting, which both surface at UC yet admit remedies upstream of the symptom, a tighter FνF_{\nu} at FA [9] and replay in EG. Long-cycle drift compounds the first three modes within one task family and forms no sixth mode. The agent-edge extension into UC, absent from the table, surfaces through erroneous writes, within a single pass in Mobile-Agent-E [162] and across later rollouts in SEAR [20]. With existing loops running only a few rounds, these mechanisms are inferred from within-run and fixed-loop evidence, and the reading stops at the cycle boundary.

Scenario Exposure.   The scenarios engage these paths unequally. In reasoning, a learned proposer extends the agent edge into σω\sigma_{\omega} and pass-rate curricula open the goal edge [208, 209], both inviting curriculum collapse. Reasoning and generation both extend the agent edge into FA through self-referential verifiers, yet the outcome follows F¯\bar{F}: under reasoning’s high ceiling, Fν(k)F_{\nu}^{(k)} drifts below F¯\bar{F}, whereas under generation’s low ceiling, compounding hacking sets in unless a frozen judge cuts that extension. In navigation and manipulation, task or environment changes drive shift and forgetting along the environment path and agent edge, and costly rollouts limit the EG resampling that counters them. Coupling thus extends the asymmetry across cycles.

IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning

Multimodal reasoning occupies the quadrant of Figure 3 in which neither ceiling is low, its rollouts being single decoding passes and its short answers admitting exact match against a pre-collected or computed reference. Training against pre-collected keys under a stationary sampler forms a fixed loop, from which self-evolving methods depart along two branches. Weight-updating loops mostly pose their own questions or train on unlabeled ones, letting the agent’s outputs supply most answers and tying the evaluator to the model it trains, which makes the realized fidelity Fν(k)F_{\nu}^{(k)}, not F¯\bar{F}, the binding factor. Training-free loops keep a frozen VLM with the key or a program and let the agent write the skills or tools it reuses, several gating each write against a validation reference, moving the cost of self-reference to the frozen writer. Reported loops run within one training run, over up to nine rounds of weight updates or sixteen of training-free writes, or over one pass of a benchmark stream.

IV-A EG Bound by Informative Goals

Experience generation in multimodal reasoning draws goals that pair a visual input (an image, a video clip, or frames of a 3D scene) with a question whose short final answer admits an equivalence check. The task families center on visual question answering over mathematical, chart, and diagram inputs [240, 241, 242], extending to pairwise quality judgments [211], temporally grounded video questions [160, 127], metric spatial questions over 3D scenes [235], and physical dynamics in videos [239, 226, 209]. These goals come from a dataset, a fixed generator, or generative roles of the agent, and in weight-updating loops the solver typically answers each goal in KkK_{k} independent decoding passes, occasionally with tool calls, yielding a 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} that groups answers to the same question, whereas training-free loops run the frozen VLM on each goal with its current skills, tools, or notes. Table VII summarizes the self-evolving methods that satisfy the conditions of Sec. II-C.

Quantity and Quality Constraints.   Experience generation is bound by quality at saturation (Table III), the task structure leaving quantity slack. A rollout is a single decoding pass over a static input, an episode with T=1T\!=\!1 except where tool calls precede the answer [216, 232, 228, 225, 220, 224], and leaves no side effect to revert, keeping both interaction cost and recoverability from lowering K¯\bar{K}. Information gain, in contrast, arises in single-answer episodes only from goals whose pass rate under the current solver lies strictly between zero and one. A dataset or a fixed generator bounds the supply of such goals by how many lie near the edge of the current agent’s competence, a number that depends on the backbone’s pretraining and, by the mechanism that stalls self-play [131], shrinks as the agent masters these goals.

Self-Posed Goals.   Larger groups do not appear to substitute for informative goals under self-consistency rewards, which lose contrast as groups grow, and loops raise the information gain instead by letting the agent pose its goals or by reweighting goals by pass rate, at a cost paid in feedback. Reported group sizes stay between four and ten rollouts per goal despite cheap decoding passes [7, 216, 6, 22, 8, 218, 234, 126, 127, 232, 215], and EvoLMM finds its self-consistency reward best at four to six samples, reporting over-consensus collapse at twelve [22], consistent with the reward, not the cost, limiting KkK_{k}. The agent enters σω\sigma_{\omega} either as a generative role within Φθ\Phi_{\theta} that synthesizes the question beside the solver, and in some loops the visual input, or through a rule that reweights dataset or generator goals by the solver’s pass rate, alone in SyncLoop [208] or on top of a learned proposer [237, 239, 209]. Proposer-solver loops after R-Zero [243] reward goals of intermediate solver agreement through terms that vanish with pg​(1−pg)p_{g}(1-p_{g}) [234, 126], adding diversity terms against a narrowing of goals [127, 5]. These rewards are computed in FA yet reshape the goal distribution of EG. In VisPlay, a trained Questioner lifts Qwen2.5-VL-3B from 30.61 to 44.16 after one round against 33.77 for an untrained Challenger [5], a comparison that attributes about three quarters of the gain to learning the role. The gain is paid in feedback, where a self-posed question lacks a key unless a program computes its answer, leaving the answer to the agent’s own outputs.

IV-B FA Bound by Realized Fidelity

Each cycle hands feedback acquisition groups of short answers to the same question, or the tool-calling episodes of a frozen agent, and the loops score each answer against one or more of three references (Table VII). The agent’s own outputs (a), through a majority vote, a self-judgment, the proposer’s answer, or consistency under image transformations, score self-posed or unlabeled questions [22, 5, 23]. An answer computed by task generation (e) scores questions whose answers programs, game rules, a geometric environment, or a physics engine determine [64, 218, 235, 239], and a pre-collected key (b) scores labeled sets [221, 223, 225]. Weight-updating methods mostly turn scores into group-normalized rewards for GRPO-style updates or into preference pairs for DPO [7, 5, 213, 214], whereas training-free methods use them to admit skills, tools, or notes into a library [146, 225, 222].

Fidelity and Localization Constraints.   Feedback acquisition is bound by realized fidelity (Table IV), its attainable fidelity being high and localization imposing little. A short answer admits exact match against a reference fixed outside the agent and leaves no channel unchecked, and without a key the program-computed answers of VQS stay correct on 94.4% of retained questions among 500 human-audited ones [64], a lower bound on F¯\bar{F} under the conversion of Sec. III-C. Consensus already falls below this bound within one round, with 24% of retained majority-vote labels and 18% of retained model-judge labels wrong in the same audit [64]. Across rounds, externally estimated pseudo-label accuracy falls from 72.0 to 61.0 over three iterations in VisPlay [5] and from 64.5 to 37.5 over five in Video-Zero [160], declines that bear on Fν(k)F_{\nu}^{(k)} only jointly with rising question difficulty, to which VisPlay attributes its own. Gaming resistance of the vote under long optimization remains untested here, whereas prolonged training against a majority-vote self-reward in text-only reasoning ends in reward hacking and abrupt collapse [244]. Single-answer episodes fix Lν=1L_{\nu}\!=\!1, the step-level agreement of iReasoner refining credit only within the output [170], and only the short tool-integrated episodes of Agent0-VL, scored as a whole [216], leave credit coarser.

Vote Preconditions and Evaluator Drift.   With localization free, every deficit of feedback acquisition is a fidelity deficit, and self-derived rewards make that fidelity a property of the model being trained. A vote recovers the model’s belief and tracks RR only where answers admit an equivalence relation and the pretrained prior concentrates on the correct answer [80, 132], discrete answers supplying the first condition and the backbone, not the task structure, deciding the second. Within these conditions the reward form matters, TTRV lowering accuracy on four of five VQA benchmarks under a hard majority-vote reward and raising it on all five under a frequency-proportional reward with entropy control [171]. The evaluators further differ in whether they move with the policy: votes over current samples, parameter-sharing supervisors [126], and self-judging models [214] keep the agent edge into FA, judges frozen at the initial model cut it [212, 230], and the moving-average verifier of Trinity lags the policy by construction [231]. A frozen evaluator still shares the prior of the policies descended from it, removing drift but not a fixed bias, and reports under differing numbers of rounds leave the designs uncompared. Answers fixed outside the agent, by a key or a program, restore F¯\bar{F} only for labeled sets and program-computable families, the same restriction that experience generation imposes on the goals.

IV-C UC Bound by Retention

Update consolidation in multimodal reasoning persists the scored experience in two forms, weight updates and training-free writes (Table VII). Weight-updating methods write Φθ\Phi_{\theta} with an update rule fixed before the loop, through group-relative policy gradients, preference optimization, or fine-tuning, either once per round over two to nine reported rounds [5, 160, 64, 235, 238, 209, 214] or continuously within a single training run. Training-free methods keep a frozen VLM and let the agent write text or code into skill and tool libraries [146, 223, 225, 220, 227], memory cards or notes [219, 222, 226], or harnesses of tools, skills, and execution code [224, 233], over benchmark streams or, in VisualEvolve, up to sixteen rounds, whereas a separate o4-mini abstracts the tool library of TVP [217]. MetaForge alone combines the two, registering validated tools that its policy forges during GRPO into a persistent library [228].

Retention and Generalization Constraints.   Update consolidation is bound by retention (Table V), inferred from non-monotone curves, not a measured loss, whereas generalization, though reported, is confounded with the backbone prior. No method measures retention on earlier-round goals, and the closest evidence, per-round scores on a fixed benchmark suite, traces the increment 𝒥k+1−𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k+1}-\mathcal{J}_{k} of Eq. 6 over the evaluation distribution, not the trained goals. These curves rise monotonically in Agent0-VL [216] but peak or dip mid-run elsewhere [8, 5], while single benchmarks reverse more often, MM-Vet falling from 48.62 to 38.07 over three VisPlay iterations as the average rises [5]. Among weight-updating methods, only ISR-DPO and Marvo run beyond five rounds, the former gaining through its ninth iteration [214] and the latter degrading after about the fifth or sixth of eight [232]. Parametric writes generalize more freely, reaching any goal that activates the updated weights and lifting standard benchmarks after training on synthesized questions [7, 5, 22]. These gains are consistent with elicitation of the backbone prior, most weight-updating methods resting on Qwen2.5-VL or Qwen3-VL, the family whose text-only counterparts gain even under spurious rewards [204]. V-Zero offers a partial control, reaching 51.9 against 50.8 for supervised GRPO on the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone [7], and only an equal-budget non-evolving baseline would separate self-evolution from elicitation. Non-parametric writes act only when retrieved, and their transfer is tested directly, EvoSpatial evaluating libraries frozen after one benchmark on 18 others [220] and VideoEvoHarness moving an evolved harness to a second backbone [233].

Reference-Gated Writes.   Consolidation inherits its exposure from the first two stages, and the two forms of writing differ in how they guard against it. Where the evaluator moves with the policy or a proposer supplies the goals, a parametric write is scored and driven by quantities that change with the update itself, and the update rule accepts every scored step without a fixed reference that could reveal a later round erasing an earlier gain. Several training-free methods gate their writes against such a reference, admitting a skill or change only on a validation or held-out gain [146, 233], promoting a skill-tool pair only on a strict gain over its training sample [225], rolling back note edits that do not raise batch accuracy [222], or selecting snapshots on fixed validation or development sets [223, 224], whereas TVP checks a new tool only against the outputs of the programs it replaces [217]. A guard on retention thus exists only where gated training-free writes keep a fixed reference.

IV-D Limits and Preconditions

Bottleneck Attribution.   The binding bottlenecks of feedback and consolidation arise from self-reference, not from task structure. Both ceilings are slack for any learning loop, and a fixed loop that trains against pre-collected keys, as M-STAR does [152], scores its rollouts at the fidelity of an exact match. The weight-updating branch gives up this reference to pose and answer its own questions, its answers coming from the agent’s own outputs, whose realized fidelity falls below F¯\bar{F}, and its parametric writes lacking a fixed reference against which a later round could be checked. The training-free branch keeps the key or a validation set and admits self-reference only through the update, shifting the cost to the writer, whose frozen backbone both diagnoses a bottleneck and writes its remedy, its capability bounding both, a limitation that Dynamo reports for itself [225]. Self-reference repays part of this cost in experience generation, where a learned proposer relieves the saturation of fixed goal supplies and accounts for most of the first-round gain of VisPlay [5]. The few cross-round audits report declines confounded with rising question difficulty, and a large question-answering prior in the backbones may account for part of the gains in both branches, disqualifying the least constrained cell as a clean baseline for the other scenarios. This attribution rests on the stage evidence and on the provenance of each method in Table VII, not on a controlled comparison with fixed loops.

Cross-Cycle Degradation.   Across cycles, self-reference exposes multimodal reasoning to degradations that a fixed loop with keys avoids. On the goal side, learned proposers extend the agent edge into σω\sigma_{\omega} and pass-rate curricula open the goal edge [208, 237, 239, 209], both inviting curriculum collapse. On the feedback side, self-derived rewards extend the agent edge into FA, inviting compounding reward hacking, and training on self-labeled answers invites model collapse along the edge into the rollout policy. The extension of training-free writers into UC remains untested, and cross-round evidence reduces to the Vision-Zero plateau, where a self-derived signal stops informing updates [218], and the late-round decline of Marvo [232], with per-round reversals of single benchmarks fitting hacking and forgetting alike.

Presupposed Resources.   The mechanisms of multimodal reasoning presuppose resources that its short, discrete answers supply. Majority votes and agreement-based proposer rewards presuppose answers that admit an equivalence relation [22, 234, 126], program-computed answers presuppose a program that determines the answer at task generation [64], and reference-gated writes presuppose a key or validation set held outside the writer [146, 225].

V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation

Multimodal generation occupies the quadrant of Figure 3 in which only the fidelity ceiling is low, an open-ended image or video having no reference output to be checked against outside sub-families such as object counts, rendered text, or program-drawn charts. Training against learned preference scorers fixed before the loop forms a fixed loop that this ceiling already binds, such scorers being exploitable under optimization [245, 129]. Weight-updating loops mostly derive the verifier from the agent, leaving the ceiling unchanged but letting the verifier’s bias move with the policy and exposing the loop to compounding reward hacking. Training-free loops mostly let a frozen backbone judge its own outputs and write its memory or skills, sharing one bias between judge and writer. Reported loops run within one training run, over at most five rounds, or over one pass of a task stream.

V-A EG Bound by Checkable Prompts

In multimodal generation, experience generation draws prompts as goals, paired with a source image in editing, and the outputs are images, videos, 3D scenes, charts, diagrams, or educational animations. The task families center on compositional text-to-image prompts [128, 12, 11], extending to aesthetic prompt optimization [246, 247], text rendering [245], safety [248], charts [191], text-to-video generation [249, 250], image editing [251, 252], and diagrams, 3D scenes, method illustrations, and animations built through tool chains [253, 254, 255, 256]. These goals come from a fixed pool or from generative roles of the agent, and weight-updating loops sample KkK_{k} outputs per prompt in one pass each, whereas training-free loops run a frozen agent through a workflow of tool calls, renders, and edits. Table IX summarizes the self-evolving methods that satisfy the conditions of Sec. II-C.

Quantity and Quality Constraints.   Experience generation is bound by quality at the coverage of checkable prompts (Table III), the task structure leaving quantity slack. A rollout costs one sampling pass or an offline tool chain [103] and leaves no side effect to revert, with reported group sizes of three to sixteen samples per prompt [128, 129, 13, 9, 257, 245]. Information gain, in contrast, runs out at the edge of what a check can score, not at the edge of the agent’s competence as in multimodal reasoning. Fixed pools come from benchmark categories whose attributes a detector, OCR, or a VQA model scores, such as those of GenEval and T2I-CompBench [128, 129, 11, 10], and a learning loop drives pass rates on such a pool toward one, where pg​(1−pg)p_{g}(1-p_{g}) approaches zero, as the fixed loop Flow-GRPO raises SD3.5-M from 0.63 to 0.95 on GenEval [195]. Open-ended prompts would still separate good outputs from poor ones under RR, yet no check fixed before the loop scores them, leaving the loop unable to draw information from them. Loops drawing every round from one prompt distribution report diminishing gains by about the third round, consistent with this saturation [12, 248].

Checkable Goal Composition.   A larger group adds samples of a prompt without extending the checkable pool, and loops raise 𝔼⁡[I𝒜k]\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}] instead by letting the agent compose or reselect goals, at a cost paid in fidelity once the goals leave what a fixed check scores. Built-in checks keep composed goals within checkable sub-families, fixing answers at prompt construction in UniRL [128], decomposing each prompt into yes/no questions in SILMM [12], and restricting the specifications that RSI in UMMs plans from its own failures to charts that program execution verifies [191]. Goals beyond these sub-families fall to frozen external judges [258, 259, 260], whereas ASG poses understanding questions over unlabeled images, scored by the agreement of its own answers across framings at a fidelity that moves with the policy [40], and reselection stays within the pool, InternalGap regenerating the prompts that yielded no accepted image [11]. Controlled returns are reported only for built-in checks and external judges, RSI in UMMs reaching 59.0% on charts after four rounds against 46.3% for longer training on its original data and leading a fixed distribution of equally many verified charts in every round [191], and RSIgen gaining 4.7, 3.1, and 2.2 points over curricula compiled from frozen sources across its three attempts [260].

V-B FA Bound by Attainable Fidelity

Each cycle hands feedback acquisition a group of outputs for the same prompt or the renders of one workflow, and the loops score each output as a whole (Table IX). The scores come from the agent itself (a), through the generator’s confidence, its understanding branch, a lagged, snapshot, or co-trained judge, or the frozen backbone that runs the workflow, or from outside it, through an external judge (b) or program execution (e). Weight-updating methods mostly turn scores into group-normalized rewards for GRPO-style updates or into preference pairs for DPO [9, 129, 13, 12, 246], whereas training-free methods receive verbal critiques, checklist scores, or pass/fail verdicts [254, 253, 264, 103] that trigger repairs within an episode and gate persistent writes.

Fidelity and Localization Constraints.   Feedback acquisition is bound by the fidelity ceiling (Table IV), to which signal source, channel coverage, and gaming resistance each contribute, while localization imposes little. An image admits no equivalence check against a fixed reference, leaving learned scorers and model judges, whose agreement with humans on open-ended content can turn negative, the frozen reviewer of ManimAgent correlating with blind ratings of 37 educational videos at r=−0.17r\!=\!-0.17 [256]. Instruments fixed before the loop score parts of the objective, such as detectors, OCR, and PickScore in Flow-GRPO [195] and HPS-v2.1, CLIP, and VideoAlign in DanceGRPO [267], and Flow-GRPO raises PickScore and OCR accuracy while human raters judge its images below the base model in quality [245]. Under optimization, IRIS attributes the realism drop of its HPSv2-trained baseline to reward hacking [129]. Only sub-families with a closed-form predicate escape the ceiling, RSI in UMMs gaining more on charts from execution-verified data than from the model’s own best-rated images [191]. Localization stays near Lν=1L_{\nu}\!=\!1, a single sampling pass forming one action and tool-orchestrated systems scoring renders with execution errors as their chief step-level signal [256, 103].

Verifier Dependence on the Policy.   With localization nearly free, every deficit of feedback acquisition is a fidelity deficit, and the methods differ in how far the verifier depends on the policy it scores. A verifier that depends on the current policy keeps the agent edge into FA, letting Fν(k)F_{\nu}^{(k)} move with each update and inviting compounding reward hacking, whereas weaker dependence slows or cuts that edge and leaves a bias fixed across cycles. Generator confidence depends on the policy entirely, and SOLACE and IRIS disagree even on its sign, rewarding higher denoising confidence and lower self-certainty, respectively [9, 129]. Understanding-branch checks hold only the prompt fixed and substitute for an external verifier only if the judging parameters are separated from the judged ones, the two directions are symmetric, and understanding exceeds generation. Shared weights violate the first condition, which KL penalties to a reference policy slow but do not remove [10, 128, 40, 13], the non-inverse relation between text-to-image and image-to-text weakens the second behind reverse-likelihood rewards [10, 257, 261], and the third, the internal gap that InternalGap converts into supervision [11], remains untested within a run [10]. Weaker dependence comes from co-evolving or lagged verifiers [246, 263, 245, 249, 262], from frozen self-verifiers [247, 251], including frozen backbones that also write the update [256, 264, 254], and from external or programmatic verifiers [259, 260, 191], and no report compares these designs at a matched number of rounds. Such designs thus trade a moving bias for a fixed one without raising F¯\bar{F}.

V-C UC Bound by Retention

Update consolidation in multimodal generation persists the scored experience in two forms, weight updates and training-free writes (Table IX). Weight-updating methods write Φθ\Phi_{\theta} with an update rule fixed before the loop, through group-relative policy gradients, preference optimization, fine-tuning, or self-distillation, either continuously within a single training run or over two to five reported rounds [246, 247, 12, 249, 191, 248]. Training-free methods keep the generator and the agent frozen and let the agent write memory [256, 265, 165, 253, 250], skill, constraint-function, concept, or middleware libraries [264, 254, 103, 255], or routing records [258], over a task stream or up to five rounds. ImageRSI alone combines the two, admitting experience to a library while retraining its judge and not its generator [262].

Retention and Generalization Constraints.   Update consolidation is bound by retention (Table V), documented within runs and in RSI in UMMs over at most four rounds, whereas generalization is mostly untested and not shown to fail. Only RSI in UMMs measures retention on earlier-round goals, exact category text on an earlier vocabulary falling from 72% to 60% once a round replaces that vocabulary and recovering when later rounds keep half of the old specifications, while general understanding, which the chart goals do not exercise, erodes by 2.6 points on MMBench [191].
